paragraphs.text: Mitochondrial myopathy with lactic acidosis is an autosomal recessive mitochondrial disorder caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in PNPLA8, which encodes the mitochondrial calcium-independent phospholipase A2-gamma (iPLA2-gamma). The first molecularly characterized patient, reported by Saunders et al. (2015), had a suspected mitochondrial myopathy with progressive muscle weakness, hypotonia, seizures, poor weight gain, and lactic acidosis. Subsequent reports broadened the phenotype; Nakamura et al. (2024) described PNPLA8-related neurologic disease as a continuum ranging from developmental and/or degenerative epileptic-dyskinetic encephalopathy, at the most severe end with congenital microcephaly, to childhood-onset neurodegeneration, and Burnyte et al. (2023) described a milder adolescent-onset form with cerebellar ataxia and peripheral neuropathy.

paragraphs.text: Mastaglia et al. (1980) described a 23-year-old man with a mitochondrial myopathy who had a high-output circulatory state and cardiomyopathy that had resulted in cardiac insufficiency 22 years before presentation of the skeletal myopathy. Venous lactate levels were elevated, and severe lactic acidosis developed at one stage of the illness. Electron microscopy of muscle showed various mitochondrial abnormalities and accumulation of neutral lipids, which was confirmed histochemically and by thin-layer chromatography. The metabolic defect was not defined.

paragraphs.text: Saunders et al. (2015) reported a 7-year-old girl (CMH193) evaluated for a suspected mitochondrial myopathy with dystonia, abnormal gait, and abnormal muscle biopsy. She was asymptomatic in the first year and met developmental milestones, although toe-walking was noted. At age 2 she had a positive Gowers sign, and by age 3 years she could no longer walk. Fine motor skills declined and speech became dysarthric. She had proximal muscle weakness, tight heel cords, and generalized mildly increased tone; weakness and dysmetria progressed, and hypotonicity progressed to spasticity. She later developed complex partial seizures with recurrent left temporal lobe spikes on EEG. She had a very lean body habitus and developed significant lactic acidosis requiring bicarbonate supplementation, with a consistently elevated anion gap since age 5. At age 7, blood lactate (3.8-5.6 mmol/L; normal 0.7-2.1) and pyruvate (0.18-0.32 mmol/L; normal 0.08-0.16) were elevated on multiple occasions, with lactate:pyruvate ratios of 17.5-21.1; creatine phosphokinase and the plasma acylcarnitine profile were normal. CSF studies at age 6 showed deficiency of 5-methyltetrahydrofolate. Brain MRI at 33 months showed subtle increased signal in the medial globus pallidus bilaterally, which was no longer seen 2 years later. Muscle biopsy at age 4 showed variable fiber size with isolated small atrophic fibers but no ragged red fibers; electron microscopy showed disarray of cristae, globular dense osmiophilic inclusions, and subsarcolemmal aggregates of abnormal mitochondria with concentric lamellar membranes, suggestive of degenerating mitochondria, as well as increased secondary lysosomes.

paragraphs.text: Shukla et al. (2018) reported 2 unrelated girls. Patient 1, of Indian origin, was the second child of consanguineous parents. She was evaluated on postnatal day 6 for congenital microcephaly and seizures; birth weight was 2410 g (-2 SD), length 48 cm (-1 SD), and head circumference 29 cm (-4 SD). She had multifocal clonic seizures from the second day of life and spasticity of all 4 limbs. Brain MRI showed microcephaly with a simplified gyral pattern, hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, a prominent cisterna magna with hypoplastic cerebellum, and brainstem atrophy, and MR spectroscopy showed an elevated lipid-lactate peak. Patient 2, born to nonconsanguineous parents (India/Fiji), developed normally until about 13 months of age, then regressed with episodes of epilepsia partialis continua and difficult-to-control focal seizures. Her development stagnated at an 8-month level, she was nonverbal, required gastrostomy feeding, and developed acquired microcephaly (head circumference 49 cm, -4.7 SD, at age 15 years), choreiform movements, dystonia, proximal muscle weakness, absent muscle stretch reflexes, and severe contractures. Serial MRI showed progressive volume loss in the cerebellum, brainstem, parietal and occipital lobes, and corpus callosum, with a persistently elevated lipid-lactate peak on MR spectroscopy. Muscle biopsy showed enlarged, irregularly shaped mitochondria with surrounding membrane whorls and disrupted cristae. Echocardiography showed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with subaortic stenosis, blood lactate was elevated on several occasions, and visual evoked potentials showed severely reduced amplitudes with prolonged latencies.

paragraphs.text: Burnyte et al. (2023) described 2 adult sibs, a brother and sister, with slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia and peripheral neuropathy. Sibling A, a 49-year-old man, developed weakness and distal muscle atrophy of the lower limbs at age 14 years, accompanied by ataxia and gait disturbance; he could not walk without assistance from age 17 and became nonambulant at age 44. He had tetraparesis, muscle wasting, absent lower limb reflexes, foot deformities, bilateral Babinski signs, marked dysmetria, and mild length-dependent hypoesthesia; at 45 years he had mild dysarthria and horizontal nystagmus, with a Mini-Mental State Examination score of 30/30. Nerve conduction studies showed sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy, and brain MRI showed mild cerebellar atrophy. Sibling B developed difficulty walking and lower limb weakness at age 14 years; at 21 years she had distal limb atrophy, absent lower limb reflexes, bilateral Babinski signs, severe axial ataxia, and appendicular dysmetria, with normal cognition and axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Neither sib had visual, auditory, cardiac, or liver dysfunction, and the authors interpreted the phenotype as milder than those previously reported.

paragraphs.text: Nakamura et al. (2024) reported 14 individuals (6 male and 8 female) with neurologic manifestations from 12 unrelated families, aged 3 days to 33 years at last assessment. Common features were central hypotonia (13 of 13), dystonia (8 of 12), seizures (10 of 14), and cerebellar atrophy (12 of 12). Eight patients (families 1-8) had congenital microcephaly (5 of 7), global developmental delay without attainment of milestones (7 of 7), peripheral spasticity (7 of 8), and seizure onset within 7 months of age (8 of 8), with a simplified gyral pattern (6 of 6), pontocerebellar hypoplasia (7 of 7), and severe progressive cerebral cortical atrophy (5 of 5). In contrast, 4 patients (families 11-12) had relatively mild features: all attained walking, 3 of 4 had ataxia, all had regression of milestones, 3 of 4 had mild or no intellectual disability, and brain MRI showed little or no cerebral cortical volume loss but progressive cerebellar atrophy. Patients from families 9 and 10 showed intermediate severity. Combining these patients with 11 previously reported individuals from 8 families (25 individuals from 20 families), the authors concluded that PNPLA8-related neurologic disease forms a continuum ranging from developmental and/or degenerative epileptic-dyskinetic encephalopathy to childhood-onset neurodegeneration.

paragraphs.text: Nakamura et al. (2024) identified biallelic ultra-rare PNPLA8 variants in 14 patients from 12 unrelated families, found by proband-only or trio exome or genome sequencing with Sanger segregation analysis; families 7 and 8 had been reported previously without details, family 7 by Denommé-Pichon et al. (2022). Of 14 variants, 12 were novel: 4 nonsense, 5 frameshift, 3 intronic near an exon-intron boundary, and 2 missense, all with population frequencies below 0.001%. In lymphoblastoid cells from patient 1, the c.1625+3_1625+6del variant caused skipping of exons 6 to 8, and his skin fibroblasts showed a significant reduction of the 77-kD PNPLA8 isoform. The splice-site variants c.2075-2A-G and c.1684-2A-G were predicted to abolish splice acceptor sites. Overall, 12 of the 14 individuals carried combinations of nonsense, frameshift, and splice-site variants, suggesting loss of function. A frameshift identified in a severely affected patient (p.Glu296Lysfs*6) also resulted in a null effect in fibroblasts. The authors also identified 2 individuals from 2 unrelated Iranian families in a non-neurologic cohort, one with optic atrophy and one with nonsyndromic hearing loss, who were homozygous for distinct N-terminal frameshift variants affecting only the largest (88-kD) isoform; in the optic atrophy family, an affected sib was heterozygous, and the authors considered the significance of these variants undetermined.

agent.process_note: Read all 10 files: full texts of Saunders 2015, Shukla 2018, Burnyte 2023 and Nakamura 2024 (all 574 lines, in parts); abstracts of Mastaglia 1980, Mancuso 2009, Masih 2021, Denommé-Pichon 2022, Abdel-Hamid 2024; title only for Hackett 1973. Grepped Nakamura for variant nomenclature and prior-report citations. No HGNC reference data was supplied, so the PNPLA8 MIM number was omitted; the 7q31 location comes from Shukla 2018. Gaps: the Masih abstract gives no protein change; the Abdel-Hamid abstract gives no zygosity for R411X or V520D; Nakamura's per-patient genotypes are in the supplement, which was not available; the Denommé-Pichon abstract does not mention PNPLA8, so it is referenced only through Nakamura. Saunders (c.1975_1976delAG/p.Leu659AlafsX4, NM_001256011.1) and Shukla (c.2275_2276delCT/p.Leu759AlafsTer4, NM_001256007.1) use different transcripts, and no paper equates them, so they are listed as separate variants. Shukla gives patient 1's birth weight as 2410 g in the text but 2500 g in the table; the text value was used.
